findings.claim: The new branch returns a non-zero result when `a` and `b` are the same wildcard string, making the comparator non-reflexive/asymmetric (compareKey(TAIL, TAIL) === -1 and compareKey(ONLY, ONLY) === 1).
findings.rationale: With `a === TAIL_WILDCARD_REG_EXP_STR` and `b === TAIL_WILDCARD_REG_EXP_STR`, the ternary yields -1; symmetrically the reversed call also yields -1, which violates the contract that equal elements compare to 0. Likewise two `ONLY_WILDCARD` keys both yield 1. In practice this may be harmless if the caller only sorts unique object keys or short-circuits on `a === b` earlier in the function (the top of the function isn't shown), but if that guard doesn't exist the sort order becomes implementation-defined/unstable. Medium-low confidence that it is reachable; worth a guard such as `if (a === b) return 0` before the wildcard block.

findings.claim: Behavior change: the only-wildcard (`.*`) no longer always sorts last, which reorders route matching priority relative to the tail wildcard.
findings.rationale: Previously any wildcard key compared as greater than everything else, so `.*` and the tail wildcard were ordered only by the fallback/stable-sort behavior. Now `.*` is explicitly placed before the tail wildcard. This changes the generated RegExp alternation order and therefore which route wins for paths matched by both `/foo/*` style and tail-wildcard patterns. Assuming this is the intent of the change, but existing callers relying on the old precedence (e.g. `/:x/*` vs `/:x` tail behavior) could see different matches; worth covering with a test for a route set containing both wildcard forms at the same node.
